title: Lawyers Say Midterm Result Brings No Immediate H-1B Relief
excerpt: Immigration lawyers and analysts say the new Congress can scrutinise H-1B restrictions and block tighter bills, but the fee, the weighted lottery and green-card dates all sit outside a simple election result.
body:
• Lawyers say no H-1B rule changes automatically on January 3, 2027, when the new Congress convenes — fees, selection and processing are set by executive action, agency rules and the courts.
  • The $100,000 fee on new H-1B petitions came from a presidential proclamation, not a statute, so ending it would take legislation, a new executive action, rulemaking or a court ruling.
  • The weighted lottery stays in force: Level I selection odds were estimated at about 15.29%, against a previous average of 29.59%, so wage level still matters for the March registration cycle.
  • India's EB-2 final action date in the November 2026 Visa Bulletin is November 1, 2013, and EB-3 is January 22, 2014 — the election does not move those dates.

Immigration lawyers are telling Indian H-1B holders and applicants not to expect quick relief from the midterm result, even though the new Congress will have more power to question the administration's restrictions. The assessment, reported by Business Standard under the headline that the results are unlikely to bring immediate H-1B relief, is echoed across the post-election coverage: scrutiny is likely to increase, but the rules themselves do not change with the vote.

Ritika Gupta, CEO and Global Education Mentor at Aaera, put the mechanism plainly in comments reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. Immigration policy, she noted, is shaped by presidential orders, legislative initiatives, Department of Homeland Security approvals and USCIS practice, not by congressional composition alone.

"Even if the political landscape changes, immigration laws will not undergo immediate changes."

— Ritika Gupta, CEO and Global Education Mentor, Aaera

What Congress can and cannot do

What a new majority can do, analysts say, is hold hearings, investigate the economic effects of the restrictions, use funding leverage and make it harder for restrictive bills to advance. Two Republican proposals illustrate the point. The End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026, introduced by Senators Tim Sheehy and Bernie Moreno with a House companion, would pause new H-1B issuance for three years, while Senator Jon Husted's Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act sits in the Senate Judiciary Committee. Neither has become law, and both face a harder path in the new Congress.

https://x.com/VtvGujarati/status/2117995492907032752

What Congress cannot do by winning an election is reverse measures that were never laws. The $100,000 fee on certain new H-1B petitions was introduced by presidential proclamation on September 19, 2025. A change in congressional control does not automatically change that fee, and its future rests with legislation, fresh executive action, agency rulemaking or the courts, where challenges to it remain live. The same applies to processing practice at USCIS and the Department of Homeland Security, which the executive branch continues to direct.

The lottery and the queue are unchanged

The selection system applicants will face next is also an agency creation. The Department of Homeland Security published a final rule on December 29, 2025 moving H-1B selection from a random lottery to a weighted process, effective February 27, 2026. Under that system, registrations at wage Level IV enter the pool four times, Level III three times, Level II twice and Level I once. Federal Register estimates cited in the coverage put the selection probability for a Level I position near 15.29%, against a previous average of 29.59% across all registrations — a change that falls hardest on entry-level applicants, including many recent Indian graduates. An election result does not repeal that rule.

The green-card queue is similarly untouched. The State Department's November 2026 Visa Bulletin lists India's employment-based second-preference final action date as November 1, 2013, and the third-preference date as January 22, 2014. Those dates move through the monthly bulletin process, not through election night, and the result does not immediately change F-1, OPT, H-1B or adjustment-of-status requirements either.

Why employers are not waiting for Washington

Indian IT firms, meanwhile, have already adjusted to a tighter regime, which limits how much any political shift can restore. Among the seven biggest IT firms in India, H-1B employment approvals totalled 4,573 in financial year 2025, down about 37% from 2024 and about 70% from 2015, according to figures reported by The Hindu BusinessLine. Gupta said firms may not return to over-reliance on the H-1B even if the process becomes more predictable, because the sector has made a structural shift toward local hiring, offshore centres and nearshore operations.

Nitin Kumar, founder of Florida-based fashion technology company The F* Word, added a timing caution that lawyers share: even with the new Congress taking over in January, immigration may not be an immediate priority alongside unemployment, AI-led job displacement and the economy, and any policy changes could take until the second or third quarter to materialise. For applicants and employers, the practical advice from practitioners is unchanged — a detailed explainer for Indians on H-1B visas reaches the same conclusion — — plan around the rules already in force, including wage-level strategy for the next registration cycle, rather than around hoped-for relief. Indians receive more than 70% of approved H-1B petitions in a typical year, so the gap between political scrutiny and actual rule change will be felt most by them.
